label: Def:Track
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Def:Track}
Suppose that $\tau \subset S$ is a pretrack and $N = N(\tau)$.  We say
that $\tau$ is a {\em train track} if $\tau$ is compact, every
component of $\partial N$ has at least one corner and every complementary
region $T$ of $\tau$ has negative index.
head: environment

label: Def:SplitSeq
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Def:SplitSeq}
In a {\em sliding and splitting sequence} $\{ \tau_i \}$ of train
tracks each $\tau_{i+1}$ is obtained from $\tau_i$ by a slide or a
split.
head: environment

label: Def:EffPos
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Def:EffPos}
Suppose that $\alpha \subset S$ is a properly embedded arc or curve.
Then $\alpha$ is in {\em efficient position} with respect to $\tau$,
denoted $\alpha \dashv \tau$, if
\begin{itemize}
\item
every component of $\alpha \cap N$ is a tie or is carried by $\tau$ and
\item
every region $T \subset S {\smallsetminus} (N \cup \alpha)$ has negative
index or is a rectangle.
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Our notion of duality is called {\em hitting efficiently} by Penner
and Harer~\cite[page 19]{PennerHarer92}. Note that $\alpha \pitchfork \tau$
if and only if $\alpha$ is carried by some extension of the {\em dual
track} $\tau^*$, also defined in~\cite{PennerHarer92}.  Likewise, if
$\alpha \dashv \tau$ and $\alpha \cap N$ consists of carried arcs then
$\alpha$ is carried by some extension of $\tau$.
head: environment

label: Lem:Essential
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:Essential}
If $\alpha$ is a properly embedded curve or arc in efficient position
with respect to a train track $\tau \subset S$ then $\alpha$ is
essential and non-peripheral in $S$.  \qed
head: environment

label: Lem:ManyDuals
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\tau$ be a complete track extending $\sigma$~\cite[Corollary
  1.4.2]{PennerHarer92}.  Section 3.4 of~\cite{PennerHarer92} and a
dimension count gives a lamination $\lambda \pitchfork \tau$ so that
$i(\lambda, \alpha) \neq 0$ for all $\alpha \in \mathcal{C}(S)$.  Now an
argument of Kobayashi~\cite{Kobayashi88b}, refined by Luo~\cite[page
  124]{MasurMinsky99}, implies that $\mathcal{C}^*(\tau) \subset
\mathcal{C}^*(\sigma)$ has infinite diameter.
head: environment

label: Def:Wide
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Def:Wide}
A multicurve $\Delta \dashv \tau$ is {\em wide} if there is an
orientation of the components of $\Delta$ so that
\begin{itemize}
\item
for every $b \in \mathcal{B}(\tau)$, all arcs of $\Delta \cap R_b$ are to
the right of each other (see the top of Figure~\ref{Fig:Right}) and
\item
for every complementary region $T$ of $\tau$, all arcs of $\Delta \cap
T$ are to the right of each other (see the bottom of Figure~\ref{Fig:Right}).
\end{itemize}
head: environment

label: Lem:VerticesWide
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:VerticesWide}
Every vertex cycle $\alpha \in V(\tau)$ is wide.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the contrapositive.  Suppose that $\alpha$ is not wide.
Orient $\alpha$.  There are three cases.

Suppose there is a branch $b \subset \tau$ and an oriented tie $t
\subset R_b$ where $x$ and $y$ are consecutive (along $t$) points of
$\alpha \cap t$ so that the signs of intersection at $x$ and $y$ are
equal.  Let $[x,y]$ be the subarc of $t$ bounded by $x$ and $y$.
Surger $\alpha$ along $[x,y]$ to form curves $\beta, \gamma \prec
\tau$.  See Figure~\ref{Fig:Surger}.  Thus $w_\alpha = w_\beta + w_\gamma$ and
$\alpha$ is not a vertex cycle.
                                                              
                                                                  
                                   

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\labellist
\small\hair 2pt
\pinlabel {$t$} [l] at 149.1 173.6
\pinlabel {$\alpha$} [l] at 291.6 145.5
\pinlabel {$\beta$} [l] at 291.6 127
\pinlabel {$\gamma$} [l] at 291.6 37.1
\endlabellist
$$\begin{array}{c}
\includegraphics[width=5.5cm]{surger} 
\end{array}$$
\caption{Surgery when adjacent intersections have the same sign.}
\label{Fig:Surger}
\end{figure}

Suppose instead that $x, y, z$ are consecutive (along $t$) points of
$\alpha \cap t$ with alternating sign.  In this case there is again a
surgery along $[x,z]$ producing curves $\beta$ and $\gamma$.  See
Figure~\ref{Fig:Surger2} for one of the possible arrangements of $\alpha$,
$\beta$ and $\gamma$.  Again $w_\alpha = w_\beta + w_\gamma$ is a
non-trivial sum and $\alpha$ is not a vertex cycle.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\labellist
\small\hair 2pt
\pinlabel {$t$} [l] at 149.1 264.0
\pinlabel {$\alpha$} [l] at 291.6 235.9
\pinlabel {$\beta$} [l] at 291.6 217.3
\pinlabel {$\gamma$} [l] at 291.6 163.6
\endlabellist
$$\begin{array}{c}
\includegraphics[width=5.5cm]{surger2} 
\end{array}$$
\caption{Surgery when the three intersections have alternating sign.}
\label{Fig:Surger2}
\end{figure}

In the remaining case $w_\alpha(a) \leq 2$ for all $a \in \mathcal{B}$ and
there are branches $b,c \in \mathcal{B}$ where the arcs of $\alpha \cap R_b$
are to the right of each other while the arcs of $\alpha \cap R_c$ are
to the left of each other.  See Figure~\ref{Fig:Disagree} for the two ways
$\alpha$ may be carried by $\tau$.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
$$\begin{array}{c}
\includegraphics[height=2.5cm]{disagree2} \\
\includegraphics[height=2.5cm]{disagree1} 
\end{array}$$
\caption{The curve $\alpha$ meets $R_b$ and $R_c$ twice.}
\label{Fig:Disagree}
\end{figure}

If $\alpha$ is carried as in the top line of Figure~\ref{Fig:Disagree} then
surger $\alpha$ in both rectangles $R_b$ and $R_c$ as was done in
Figure~\ref{Fig:Surger}.  This shows that $w_\alpha$ is a non-trivial sum and
so $\alpha$ is not a vertex cycle.  Now suppose that $\alpha$ is
carried as in the bottom line of Figure~\ref{Fig:Disagree}.  Note that the
closure of $\alpha {\smallsetminus} (R_b \cup R_c)$ is a union of four arcs.
Two of these, $\beta'$ and $\gamma'$, meet both $R_b$ and $R_c$.
Since $S$ is orientable no tie-preserving isotopy of $N$ throws
$\beta'$ onto $\gamma'$.
                                     
Let $\alpha' \cup \alpha'' = \alpha {\smallsetminus} (\beta'
\cup \gamma')$.  Create an embedded curve $\beta$ by taking two
parallel copies of $\beta'$ and joining them to $\alpha'$ and
$\alpha''$.  Similarly create $\gamma$ by joining two parallel copies
of $\gamma'$ to the arcs $\alpha'$ and $\alpha''$.  It follows that
$w_\beta \neq w_\gamma$.  Since $2w_\alpha = w_\beta + w_\gamma$ again
$\alpha$ is not a vertex cycle.
head: environment
name: Proof of \reflem{VerticesWide}

label: Lem:Decompose
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:Decompose}
Suppose that $X \subset S$ is an essential surface and $\tau$ is a
track.  If some $\alpha \prec \tau$ ($\alpha \pitchfork \tau$) cuts $X$
then there is a vertex cycle $\beta \prec \tau$ (wide dual $\beta
\pitchfork \tau$) cutting $X$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Some multiple of $\alpha \prec \tau$ is a sum of vertices: $m \cdot
w_\alpha = \sum n_i w_i$ where $w_i$ is the integral transverse
measure for the vertex $\beta_i \in V(\tau)$.  Via a sequence of
tie-preserving isotopies of $N$ we may arrange for all of the
$\beta_i$ to realize their geometric intersection with each
other. Note that there is an isotopy representative of $\alpha$
contained inside of a small neighborhood of the union $B = \cup
\beta_i$.

To prove the contrapositive, suppose that none of the $\beta_i$ cut
$X$.  It follows that $X$ may be isotoped in $S$ to be disjoint from
$B$.  Thus $\alpha$ misses $X$, as desired.  A similar
discussion applies when $\alpha \pitchfork \tau$.
head: environment

label: Lem:Compact
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:Compact}
If $X$ is not an annulus then the induced track $\tau|X$ is compact.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Note train-routes in $\tau^X$ that are mapped properly to $S^X$ are
uniform quasi-geodesics in $S^X$~\cite[Proposition 3.3.3]{Mosher03}.
                               
Thus there is a compact core $X' \subset S^X$, homeomorphic to $X$, so
that any route meeting $S^X {\smallsetminus} X'$ has one endpoint on the
Gromov boundary of $S^X$.  It follows that $\tau|X \subset X'$.
head: environment

label: Lem:TransverseRecurrenceAC
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:TransverseRecurrenceAC}
Suppose that $\tau$ is transversely recurrent in $S$.  Then $\tau|X$
is transversely recurrent with respect to arcs and curves in $X$.
Furthermore: suppose that $\tau|X$ is transversely recurrent with
respect to arcs and curves in $X$.  If $\sigma \subset \tau|X$ is a
train track then $\sigma$ is transversely recurrent in $X$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first claim follows from the definitions.  An index argument
proves the second claim.
head: environment

label: Lem:Surgery
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:Surgery}
Suppose that $\tau$ is a track and $X \subset S$ is an essential
subsurface, yet not an annulus.  For every $\alpha \in \mathcal{A}(\tau^X)$
at least one of the following holds:
\begin{itemize}
\item
There is an arc $\beta \in \mathcal{A}(\tau^X)$ so that $\beta$ is wide and
$i(\alpha, \beta) = 0$.
\item
There is a curve $\gamma \in \mathcal{C}(\tau|X)$ so that $i(\alpha, \gamma)
\leq 2$.
\end{itemize}
The statement also holds replacing $\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{C}$ by $\mathcal{A}^*,
\mathcal{C}^*$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is modelled on that of Lemma~\ref{Lem:VerticesWide}.  If $\alpha
\prec \tau^X$ is wide we are done.  If not, as $\alpha$ is a
quasi-geodesic~\cite[Proposition 3.3.3]{Mosher03}, 
                             
orient $\alpha$ so that $\alpha$ is wide outside of a compact core for
$S^X$.  Now we induct on the total number of arcs of intersection
between $\alpha$ and rectangles $R_b \subset N(\tau^X)$ meeting the
compact core.

Let $t$ be a tie of $R_b$.  Orient $t$. Suppose that $x, y$ are
consecutive (along $t$) points of $\alpha \cap t$.  Suppose that the
sign of intersection at $x$ equals the sign at $y$.  Let $[x,y]$ be
the subarc of $t$ bounded by $x$ and $y$.  As in Lemma~\ref{Lem:VerticesWide}
surger $\alpha$ along $[x,y]$ to form an arc $\beta'$ and a curve
$\gamma$.  See Figure~\ref{Fig:Surger} with $\beta'$ substituted for $\beta$.

Note that $\gamma$ is essential in $S^X$, by an index argument.  If
$\gamma$ is non-peripheral then the second conclusion holds.  So
suppose that $\gamma$ is peripheral.  Then $\alpha$ is obtained by
Dehn twisting $\beta'$ about $\gamma$.  So $\beta'$ is properly
isotopic to $\alpha$ and has smaller intersection with $R_b$; thus we
are done by induction.

Suppose instead that $x, y, z$ are consecutive (along $t$) points of
$\alpha \cap t$, with alternating sign.  Surger $\alpha$ along $[x,z]$
to form an arc $\beta'$ and a curve $\gamma$.  See Figure~\ref{Fig:Surger2},
with $\beta'$ substituted for $\beta$, for one of the possible
arrangements of $\alpha$, $\beta'$, and $\gamma$.  Again $\gamma$ is
essential.  If $\gamma$ is non-peripheral then the second conclusion
holds and we are done.  If $\gamma$ is peripheral then, as $\alpha$
and $\beta'$ differ by a half-twist about $\gamma$, we find that
$\beta'$ is properly isotopic to $\alpha$.  Since $\beta'$ has smaller
intersection with $R_b$ we are done by induction.

All that remains is the case that $\alpha$ meets every rectangle $R_b$
in most a pair of arcs of opposite orientation. For every branch $b$
where $\alpha$ meets $R_b$ twice, choose a subarc $t_b$ of a tie in
$R_b$ so that $\alpha \cap t_b = \partial t_b$.  We call $t_b$ a {\em
chord} for $\alpha$.  For every $t_b$ there is a subarc $\alpha_b
\subset \alpha$ so that $\partial t_b = \partial \alpha_b$.  A chord $t_b$ is
{\em innermost} if there is no chord $t_c$ with $\alpha_c$ strictly
contained in $\alpha_b$.  Let $t_b$ be the first innermost chord.  Let
$\alpha'$ be the component of $\alpha {\smallsetminus} \alpha_b$ before
$\alpha_b$.  Build a route $\beta$ by taking two copies of $\alpha'$
and joining them to $\alpha_b$.  Note that $\beta \cap R_c$ is a
single arc or a pair of arcs exactly as $\alpha_b$ or $\alpha'$ meets
$R_c$.  Thus $\beta$ is wide.  Also, $\beta$ is essential: otherwise
$t_b \cup \alpha_b$ bounds a disk with index one-half, a
contradiction.  By construction $i(\alpha, \beta) = 0$ and
Lemma~\ref{Lem:Surgery} is proved.
head: environment

label: Lem:WideInAnnuli
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:WideInAnnuli}
Suppose that $X \subset S$ is an essential annulus.  If
$\mathcal{A}^{(*)}(\tau|X)$ is nonempty then $V^{(*)}(\tau|X)$ is nonempty.
Let $N = N(\tau|X)$.  If $\gamma \dashv \tau|X$ is a wide essential arc
then $\gamma$ meets each rectangle of $N$ and each region of $S^X
{\smallsetminus} N$ in at most a single arc.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the second conclusion; the first is similar.  Suppose that
$R$ is either a rectangle or region so that $\gamma \cap R$ is a pair
of arcs to the right of each other.  Let $\delta$ be an arc properly
embedded in $R {\smallsetminus} \gamma$ so that $\delta \cap \gamma = \partial
\delta$.  Let $\gamma'$ be the component of $\gamma {\smallsetminus} \partial
\delta$ so that $\partial \gamma' = \partial \delta$.  If $\gamma' \cup
\delta$ bounds a disk in $S^X$ then this disk has index one-half and
we contradict efficient position.  If $\gamma' \cup \delta$ bounds an
annulus then $\gamma$ was not essential, another contradiction.
head: environment
name: Proof of \reflem{WideInAnnuli}

label: Lem:AnnulusEquality
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:AnnulusEquality}
If $\alpha$ is not carried by $\tau|X$ then $V(\tau|X) =
\mathcal{A}(\tau|X)$.  If $\alpha$ is not dual to $\tau|X$ then $V^*(\tau|X)
= \mathcal{A}^*(\tau|X)$. \qed
head: environment

label: Lem:Combed
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:Combed}
Suppose that $\alpha \prec \tau|X$.  One side of $\alpha$ is combed if
and only if both sides are combed in the same direction if and only if
some isotopy representative of $\alpha$ is dual to $\tau|X$. \qed
head: environment

label: Thm:EffPos
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm:EffPos}
Suppose that $\xi(S) \geq 1$ and $\tau \subset S$ is a birecurrent
train track.  Suppose that $\Delta \subset \mathcal{AC}(S)$ is a multicurve.
Then efficient position for $\Delta$ with respect to $\tau$ exists and
is unique up to rectangle swaps, annulus swaps, and isotopies of $S$
preserving the foliation of $N(\tau)$ by ties.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
When $S = S_1$ is a torus, Lemma~14 of~\cite{Gueritaud09} proves the
existence of efficient position for curves with respect to Reebless
bigon tracks.  Uniqueness of efficient position follows from a slight
generalization of Section~\ref{Sec:Unique} using {\em bigon swaps}.
head: environment

label: Cor:EfficientIntersection
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{Cor:EfficientIntersection}
Suppose that $\Gamma \subset \mathcal{AC}(S)$ is a finite collection of arcs
and curves in efficient position.  Then we may perform a sequence of
rectangle swaps to realize the pairwise geometric intersection
numbers.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Gamma = \{ \gamma_i \}_{i=1}^{k}$.  By induction, the curves of
$\Gamma' = \Gamma {\smallsetminus} \{ \gamma_k \}$ realize their pairwise
geometric intersection numbers.  If $\gamma_k$ meets some $\gamma_i
\in \Gamma'$ non-minimally then by the Bigon Criterion~\cite[page
46]{FLP91} there is an innermost bigon between $\gamma_k$ and some
$\gamma_j \in \Gamma'$.  We now may reduce the intersection number
following the proof of uniqueness of efficient position.
head: environment

label: Clm:RisingFalling
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{Clm:RisingFalling}
For any route $\rho \prec \tau^\mathbb{H}$ one side of $\rho$ has infinitely
many rising branches while the other side has infinitely many falling
branches.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that there are infinitely many half-branches on both sides of
$\rho$: if not then $\partial_h N(\tau)$ would have a component without
corners, contrary to assumption.
                                                                   
                                                                
                                                            
Suppose that there are only finitely many rising branches along
$\rho$.  Then there is a curve $\gamma \prec \tau$ so that
$w_\gamma(b) \leq 1$ for every branch $b$ and so that the two sides of
$\gamma$ are combed in opposite directions.  
                       
Thus $\tau$ is not recurrent, a contradiction.  The same contradiction
is obtained if there are only finitely many falling branches along
$\rho$.
head: environment

label: Clm:Converge
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{Clm:Converge}
For any route $\rho \prec \tau^\mathbb{H}$ and for any family of half-routes
$\{ \beta_n \}$ if $\beta_n \cap \rho = \rho(n)$ then $\lim_{n \to
\infty} \beta_n(\infty) = \rho(\infty)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $x = \rho(\infty) \in \partial_\infty \mathbb{H}$.  Consider the subsequence
$\{ \beta_n \}$ where the first branch of each $\beta_n$ is falling.
Let $P_n = \rho|(-\infty, n] \cup \beta_n$, oriented away from
$\rho(-\infty)$.  Note that $P_n(\infty) = \beta_n(\infty)$.  Recall
that $\rho$ and $P_n$ are both uniformly close to
geodesics~\cite[pages 61--62]{PennerHarer92}.  Thus $P_n(\infty) \to
x$ as $n \to \infty$.
                                                              
                                                                 
                                                                      
                                     

Now consider the subsequence $\{ \beta_n \}$ where the first branch of
each $\beta_n$ is rising.  Let $P_n = \beta_n \cup \rho|[n, \infty)$
oriented towards $x$; so $P_n(\infty) = x$ for all $n$.  Note that
$P(-\infty) = \beta_n(\infty)$.  Since all complementary regions of
$\tau^\mathbb{H}$ have negative index none of the $P_n$ may cross each other.
It follows that either the $P_n$ exit compact subsets of $\mathbb{H}$, and we
are done, or the $P_n$ converge~\cite[Theorem~1.5.4]{PennerHarer92} to
$P$, a train-route with $P(\infty) = x$.  Since $P$ does not cross any
$P_n$ deduce that $P$ and $\rho$ are disjoint.  But this
contradicts~\cite[Corollary 3.3.4]{Mosher03}: train-routes that share
an endpoint must share a half-route.
head: environment

label: Clm:Cofinal
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{Clm:Cofinal}
For any distinct $z, y \in S^1$ there is a train-route $\rho$ so that
one of the intervals $\partial_\infty H^\pm(\rho)$ is contained in
$(z,y)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The endpoints of train-routes are dense in $S^1 = \partial_\infty \mathbb{H}$.
                                                          
                                                                 
                                                                      
                                                               
                                                                      
                                                                   
                                                                 
                                                                    
                                                
Fix $x \in (z, y)$ so that $x$ is the endpoint of a train-route
$\gamma$.  Since there are infinitely many rising branches along
$\gamma$ (Claim~\ref{Clm:RisingFalling}) the claim follows from the rising
case of Claim~\ref{Clm:Converge}.
head: environment

label: Clm:NearlyHalfSpace
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{Clm:NearlyHalfSpace}
The union $\mathcal{H}_{x,y}$ is contained in an $\delta$--neighborhood of
$H_{x,y}$, where $\delta$ may be taken as small as desired by choosing
appropriate $\epsilon, L$.  \qed
head: environment

label: Clm:Convex
title: Claim
body_md:
\label{Clm:Convex}
$\mathbb{H} {\smallsetminus} \mathcal{H}_{x,y}$ is closed and $\epsilon'$--convex, where
$\epsilon'$ may be taken as small as desired by choosing appropriate
$\epsilon, L$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: This is proved in detail on pages 122-123 of~\cite{MasurMinsky99}.
head: environment

label: Clm:Accumulation
title: Claim
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Pick a sequence of subintervals $(x_n, y_n) \subset (x,y)$ so that
$x_n, y_n \to x$ as $n \to \infty$.  By Claim~\ref{Clm:Cofinal} for every $n$
there is a route $\rho_n$ and a half-plane $H_n = H(\rho_n)$ so that
$\partial_\infty H_n \subset (x_n, y_n)$.  It follows that $H_n \subset
\mathcal{H}_{x,y}$.  Let $r_n$ be any bi-infinite geodesic perpendicular to
$\partial H_{x,y}$ and meeting $H_n$.  Thus $r_n \to x$ as $n \to \infty$.
By Claim~\ref{Clm:NearlyHalfSpace} the intersection $r_n \cap \partial (\mathbb{H}
{\smallsetminus} \mathcal{H}_{x,y})$ is nonempty, and we are done.
head: environment

label: Lem:Basis
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:Basis}
For any non-parabolic point $x \subset S^1$ there is a sequence of
train-routes $\{ \rho_n \}$ with associated half-planes $\{ H(\rho_n)
\}$ forming a neighborhood basis for $x$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $y, z$ be arbitrary points of $S^1$ so that $x, y, z$ are ordered
counterclockwise.  It suffices to construct a train-route separating
$x$ from $(y,z)$.

First assume that $x$ is the endpoint of a route $\rho$.
Claim~\ref{Clm:RisingFalling} implies that there are infinitely many rising
branches $\{ a_m \}$ on one side of $\rho$ and infinitely many falling
branches $\{ c_n \}$ on the other side.  Run half-routes $\alpha_m$
and $\gamma_n$ through $a_m$ and $c_n$; so each half-route meets
$\rho$ in a single switch.  By Claim~\ref{Clm:Converge} the endpoints
converge $\alpha_m(\infty), \gamma_n(\infty) \to x$.  Thus
sufficiently large $m, n$ give a train-route
\[
\alpha_m \cup \rho|_{[m, n]} \cup \gamma_n
\]
that separates $x$ from $(y,z)$, as desired. 

For the general case consider
\[
\mathcal{K} = \mathbb{H} {\smallsetminus} (\mathcal{H}_{z,x} \cup \mathcal{H}_{x,y}).
\]
Note that $x$ is an accumulation point of $\mathcal{K}$ (by
Claim~\ref{Clm:Accumulation} and because $\mathcal{H}_{z,x}$ cannot contain points
of $\partial (\mathbb{H} {\smallsetminus} \mathcal{H}_{x,y})$).
                                    
Fix any basepoint $w \in \mathcal{K}$.  By Claim~\ref{Clm:Convex} $\mathcal{K}$ is
$\epsilon'$--convex.  Thus there is a path $r \subset \mathcal{K}$ from $w$
to $x$ which has geodesic curvature less than $\epsilon'$ at every
point.  Since $x$ is not a parabolic point the projection of $r$ to
$S$ recurs to the thick part of $S$; thus $r$ meets infinitely many
branches $\{ b_n \}$ of $\tau^\mathbb{H}$.

Suppose that $b$ is a branch of $\tau^\mathbb{H}$ lying in $\mathcal{K}$.  If
the two sides of $b$ meet $\mathcal{H}_{z,x}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{x,y}$ then $b$ is
a {\em bridge} of $\mathcal{K}$.  If the sides of $b$ meet neither
$\mathcal{H}_{z,x}$ nor $\mathcal{H}_{x,y}$ then $b$ is an {\em interior branch}
of $\mathcal{K}$.  If exactly one side of $b$ lies in $\mathcal{K}$ then $b$ is a
{\em boundary branch}.  If both sides lie in $\mathcal{H}_{z,x}$ (or both
sides lie in $\mathcal{H}_{x,y}$) then $b$ is an {\em exterior branch}.
See Figure~\ref{Fig:K} below. 

By convexity the path $r$ is disjoint from the exterior branches.
After a small isotopy the path $r$ is also disjoint from the boundary
branches, meets the interior branches transversely, and still has
geodesic curvature less than $\epsilon'$ at every point.

Now, if $r$ travels along a bridge then there are routes $\rho^\pm$
cutting off half-planes $H^\pm$ lying in $\mathcal{H}_{z,x}$ and
$\mathcal{H}_{x,y}$ respectively.  Then either $x$ is the endpoint of a
train-route or a cut and paste of $\rho^\pm$ gives the desired route
$\Gamma$ separating $x$ from $(y,z)$.  In either case we are done.
                    

So suppose that $r$ only meets interior branches $\{ b_n \}$ of
$\mathcal{K}$.  Let $\gamma_n$ be any train-route travelling along $b_n$.
If any of the $\gamma_n$ land at $x$ we are done, as above.  Supposing
not: Fixing orientations and passing to a subsequence we may assume
that $\gamma_n(\infty) \to x$ as $n \to \infty$.  There are now two
cases: suppose that for infinitely many $n$ we find that
$\gamma_n(-\infty) \in [y,z]$.  Then passing to a further subsequence
we have that $\gamma_n \to \Gamma$ where $\Gamma(\infty) =
x$~\cite[Theorem~1.5.4]{PennerHarer92}; thus $x$ is the endpoint of a
train-route and we are done as above.  The other possibility is that
for some sufficiently large $n$ both endpoints $\gamma_n(\pm\infty)$
lie in $(z, y)$.  Since $b_n$ is an interior branch $\gamma_n$
separates $x$ from $(y,z)$ and Lemma~\ref{Lem:Basis} is proved.

label: Lem:AnnulusBound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:AnnulusBound}
Suppose that $\tau$ is a birecurrent track and $X \subset S$ is an
essential annulus.  If $\tau|X \neq \emptyset$ then the diameter of
$V(\tau|X) \cup V^*(\tau|X)$ inside of $\mathcal{A}(X)$ is at most eight.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In the proof we use $V, V^*$ to represent $V(\tau|X)$ and
$V^*(\tau|X)$.  Since $\tau|X \neq \emptyset$ it follows that
$\mathcal{A}(\tau|X)$ is nonempty.  The first conclusion of
Lemma~\ref{Lem:WideInAnnuli} now implies that $V$ is nonempty.

\begin{claim*}
$V^* \neq \emptyset$.
\end{claim*}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:ManyDuals} there is a dual curve $\beta \in \mathcal{C}^*(\tau)$
so that $i(\alpha, \beta) > 0$.  Thus there is a lift $\beta' \subset
S^X$ with closure an essential arc.  Since $\tau|X \subset \tau^X$ it
follows that $\beta' \in \mathcal{A}^*(\tau|X)$.  The first conclusion of
Lemma~\ref{Lem:WideInAnnuli} now implies that $V^*$ is nonempty.
                                                                      
                                                              
                                                                      
                                            
\end{proof}

\begin{claim*}
If $\beta \in V$ and $\gamma \in V^*$ then $i(\beta, \gamma) \leq 3$.
\end{claim*}

\begin{proof}
Suppose that $i(\beta, \gamma) = n \geq 4$. Let $\{ \gamma_i
\}_{i=1}^{n-1}$ be the components of $\gamma {\smallsetminus} \beta$ with
both endpoints on $\beta$. Let $R_i$ be the components of $S^X
{\smallsetminus} (\beta \cup \gamma)$ with compact closure.  We arrange
matters so that opposite sides of $R_i$ are on $\gamma_i$ and
$\gamma_{i+1}$.  Let $R$ be the union of the $R_i$.  Since $\operatorname{index}(R) =
0$ every region $T$ of the closure of $R {\smallsetminus} N(\tau|X)$ also has
index zero and so is a rectangle.  If $T$ meets both $\gamma_i$ and
$\gamma_{i+1}$ then $\gamma$ was not wide, a contradiction.  As $n - 1
\geq 3$ any region $T$ meeting $\gamma_2$ is a compact rectangle
component of the closure of $S^X {\smallsetminus} N(\tau|X)$.  An index
argument implies that $\tau^X$ and thus $\tau \subset S$ has a
complementary region with non-negative index, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\noindent
Since $V, V^*$ are nonempty it follows that $\operatorname{diam}(V \cup V^*) \leq
8$.

label: Lem:GeneralBound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:GeneralBound}
There is a constant ${\sf K_1} = {\sf K_1}(S)$ with the following property.
Suppose that $\tau$ is a track and $X \subset S$ is an essential
subsurface (not an annulus) with $\pi_X(\tau) \neq \emptyset$.  Then
the diameter of $W(\tau^X) \cup W^*(\tau^X)$ inside of $\mathcal{AC}(X)$ is at
most ${\sf K_1}$.  Furthermore if, after isotoping $\partial X$ into efficient
position, the induced orientation on $\partial X$ is not wide then
either $\mathcal{C}(\tau|X)$ or $\mathcal{C}^*(\tau|X)$ has diameter at most two
in $\mathcal{C}(X)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In the proof we use $W, W^*, \mathcal{AC}, \mathcal{AC}^*$ to represent $W(\tau^X)$ and
so on.  Since $\pi_X(\tau) \neq \emptyset$ there is some vertex cycle
$\alpha \in V(\tau)$ so that $\alpha$ cuts $X$.  Since $\alpha$ is
wide (Lemma~\ref{Lem:VerticesWide}) there is a lift $\alpha' \prec \tau^X$
which is also wide; deduce that $W$ is nonempty.

                                                                      
                                                               

\begin{claim*}
$W^* \neq \emptyset$.
\end{claim*}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:ManyDuals} there is a dual curve $\alpha \in \mathcal{C}^*(\tau)$
cutting $X$.  By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Decompose} there is a wide dual $\beta$ that
also cuts $X$.  Thus there is a lift $\beta' \subset S^X$ with closure
an essential wide arc or wide essential, non-peripheral curve.  So
$\beta' \in W^*$ as desired.
\end{proof}

Now isotope $\partial X$ into efficient position.  Let $X'$ be the compact
component of the preimage of $X$ under the covering map $S^X \to S$.
Note that $\partial X'$ is in efficient position with respect to $\tau^X$.
Note that the covering map $S^X \to S$ induces a homeomorphism between
$X'$ and $X$.  Let $N^X = N(\tau^X) \subset S^X$ be the preimage of $N
= N(\tau)$.  Let $N' = X' \cap N^X$.  Again, the covering map induces
a homeomorphism between $N'$ and $N \cap X$.

Suppose that $\partial X$, with its induced orientation, is not wide.  If
$\partial X$ fails to be wide in $S {\smallsetminus} N(\tau)$ then there is a
properly embedded, essential arc $\gamma \subset X$ disjoint from
$N(\tau)$.  Lift $\gamma$ to $\gamma' \subset X'$.  Adjoin to
$\gamma'$ geodesic rays in $S^X {\smallsetminus} X'$ to obtain an essential,
properly embedded arc $\gamma'' \subset S^X$.  Note that $i(\gamma'',
\alpha) = 0$ for every $\alpha \in \mathcal{AC}$; only intersections in $X'$
contribute to geometric intersection number as computed in $S^X$.
This implies that $\operatorname{diam}_X(\mathcal{C}(\tau|X)) \leq 2$.  Furthermore,
$i(\gamma'', \beta) \leq 2$ for every $\beta \in W^*$.  This gives the
desired diameter bound for $W \cup W^*$.

If, instead, $\partial X$ fails to be wide in $N(\tau)$ then there is a
properly embedded, essential arc $\gamma \subset X$ that is a subarc
of a tie.  Again, lift and extend to an essential arc $\gamma''
\subset S^X$ so that $i(\gamma'', \beta) = 0$ for any $\beta \in
\mathcal{AC}^*$.  This implies that $\operatorname{diam}_X(\mathcal{C}^*(\tau|X)) \leq 2$.  We also
have $i(\gamma'', \alpha) \leq 2$ for any $\alpha \in W$. Again the
diameter is bounded.
                                                 

Now suppose that $\partial X$ is wide.  Thus, for every $b \in
\mathcal{B}(\tau)$, the rectangle $R_b$ meets $\partial X$ in at most a pair of
arcs. It follows that $N \cap X$, and thus $N'$, is a union of at most
$2|\mathcal{B}(\tau)|$ subrectangles of the form $R', R'' \subset R_b$.
Suppose that $\alpha \in W$ and $\beta \in W^*$.  Then $\alpha$ and
$\beta$ each meet a subrectangle $R'$ in at most two arcs.  Thus
$\alpha$ and $\beta$ intersect in at most four points inside of $R'$.
Thus $i(\alpha, \beta) \leq 8 |\mathcal{B}(\tau)|$ and Lemma~\ref{Lem:GeneralBound}
is proved.

label: Thm:FellowTravel
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm:FellowTravel}
For any surface $S$ with $\xi(S) \geq 1$ there is a constant ${\sf K_0} =
{\sf K_0}(S)$ with the following property: Suppose that $\{ \tau_i
\}_{i=0}^N$ is a sliding and splitting sequence of birecurrent train
tracks in $S$ and suppose that $X \subset S$ is an essential
subsurface.
\begin{itemize}
\item
For every $[a,b] \subset [0,N]$ if $[a,b] \cap I_X = \emptyset$ and
$\pi_X(\tau_b) \neq \emptyset$ then $d_X(\tau_a, \tau_b) \leq {\sf K_0}$.
\end{itemize}
Suppose $i \in I_X$.  If $X$ is an annulus:
\begin{itemize}
\item
The core curve $\alpha$ is carried by and wide in $\tau_i$.
\item
Both sides of $\alpha$ are combed in the induced track $\tau_i|X$.
\item
If $i+1 \in I_X$ then $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is obtained by taking subtracks,
slides, or at most a pair of splittings of $\tau_i|X$.
\end{itemize}
If $X$ is not an annulus:
\begin{itemize}
\item
When in efficient position
                                       
$\partial X$ is wide with respect to $\tau_i$.
\item
The track $\tau_i|X$ is birecurrent and fills $X$.
\item
If $i+1 \in I_X$ then $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is either a subtrack, a slide, or
a split of $\tau_i|X$.
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix an interval $[a,b] \subset [0,N]$.  Note that $\tau_b \prec
\tau_a$ and so $\tau_b^X \prec \tau_a^X$.  Thus $\mathcal{AC}(\tau_b^X) \subset
\mathcal{AC}(\tau_a^X)$ while $\mathcal{AC}^*(\tau_a^X) \subset \mathcal{AC}^*(\tau_b^X)$.

\begin{claim*}
If $[a,b] \cap I_X = \emptyset$ and $\pi_X(\tau_b) \neq \emptyset$
then $d_X(\tau_a, \tau_b) \leq {\sf K_0}$.
\end{claim*}

\begin{proof}
Fix, for the duration of the claim, a vertex cycle $\beta \in
V(\tau_b)$ so that $\beta$ cuts $X$.  Since $\beta$ is also carried by
$\tau_a$ there is, by Lemma~\ref{Lem:Decompose}, a vertex cycle $\alpha \in
V(\tau_a)$ cutting $X$.  Pick $\alpha' \in \pi_X(\alpha)$ and $\beta'
\in \pi_X(\beta)$.  Note Lemma~\ref{Lem:VerticesWide} implies that
$\alpha'$ is wide in $\tau_a^X$ while $\beta'$ is wide in $\tau_b^X$.
The proof divides into cases depending on the relative positions of
$a, b, m_X$ and $n_X$.

\begin{case}
Suppose $n_X < a$ or $n_X$ is undefined. 
\end{case}

Note that $\beta' \prec \tau_a^X$.  If $X$ is an annulus then since $a
\mathbin{\notin} I_X$ the diameter of $\mathcal{A}(\tau_a|X)$ is at most eight; thus
$d_X(\alpha, \beta) \leq 8$ and we are done.

Suppose that $X$ is not an annulus.  If $\beta'$ is an arc then
Lemma~\ref{Lem:Surgery} gives two cases: we may replace $\beta'$ by $\gamma$
which is either a wide arc in $\tau_a^X$ or is an essential
non-peripheral curve in $\tau_a|X$.  (If $\beta'$ is a curve then let
$\gamma = \beta'$.)  In either case Lemma~\ref{Lem:Surgery} ensures that
$i(\gamma, \beta') \leq 2$ and so $d_X(\gamma, \beta') \leq 4$.  If
$\gamma$ is an arc then both $\alpha'$ and $\gamma$ are wide so
Lemma~\ref{Lem:GeneralBound} gives $d_X(\alpha, \beta) \leq {\sf K_1} + 4$.  If
$\gamma$ is a curve pick any $\delta \in V(\tau_a|X)$.  Then
Lemma~\ref{Lem:GeneralBound} implies that $d_X(\alpha', \delta) \leq {\sf K_1}$.
Also, $a \mathbin{\notin} I_X$ implies that $d_X(\delta, \gamma) \leq 2$.  Thus
$d_X(\alpha, \beta) \leq {\sf K_1} + 6$.

\begin{case}
Suppose $b < m_X$ or $m_X$ is undefined. 
\end{case}

If $X$ is an annulus, then Lemma~\ref{Lem:AnnulusBound} gives wide duals
$\alpha^* \in V^*(\tau_a|X)$ and $\beta^* \in V^*(\tau_b|X)$ so that
$d_X(\alpha', \alpha^*), d_X(\beta', \beta^*) \leq 8$.  It follows
that the arc $\alpha^*$ also lies in $\mathcal{A}^*(\tau_b|X)$.  Since $b
\mathbin{\notin} I_X$ we have $d_X(\alpha^*, \beta^*) \leq 8$.  Thus $d_X(\alpha,
\beta) \leq 24$, as desired.

If $X$ is not an annulus, then by Lemma~\ref{Lem:GeneralBound} there is a
wide dual $\alpha^* \in W^*(\tau_a^X)$ so that $d_X(\alpha', \alpha^*)
\leq {\sf K_1}$.  Again, $\alpha^*$ is also an element of
$\mathcal{AC}^*(\tau_b^X)$ but may not be wide there.  If $\alpha^*$ is an arc
then Lemma~\ref{Lem:Surgery} gives two cases: we may replace $\alpha^*$ by
$\gamma^*$ which is either a wide dual arc to $\tau_b^X$ or is an
essential non-peripheral dual curve to $\tau_b^X$.  (If $\alpha^*$ is
a curve then let $\gamma^* = \alpha^*$.)  So $i(\alpha^*, \gamma^*)
\leq 2$ and thus $d_X(\alpha^*, \gamma^*) \leq 4$.  If $\gamma^*$ is a
wide dual arc then Lemma~\ref{Lem:GeneralBound} implies that $d_X(\gamma^*,
\beta') \leq {\sf K_1}$ and so $d_X(\alpha, \beta) \leq 2{\sf K_1} + 4$.  If
$\gamma^*$ is a dual curve then, as $b \mathbin{\notin} I_X$, any dual wide curve
$\delta^* \in V^*(\tau_b|X)$ has $d_X(\gamma^*, \delta^*) \leq 2$.
Again, Lemma~\ref{Lem:GeneralBound} implies that $d_X(\delta^*, \beta') \leq
{\sf K_1}$ and so $d_X(\alpha, \beta) \leq 2{\sf K_1} + 6$.

\begin{case}
Suppose $a \leq n_X < c < m_X \leq b$.
\end{case}

The first two cases bound $d_X(\tau_c, \tau_b)$ and $d_X(\tau_a,
\tau_c)$; thus we are done by the triangle inequality.

\begin{case}
Suppose $a \leq n_X < m_X \leq b$ and $m_X = n_X + 1$.
\end{case}

Let $c = n_X$ and $d = m_X$.  The first two cases bound $d_X(\tau_d,
\tau_b)$ and $d_X(\tau_a, \tau_c)$.  Since $V(\tau_c)$ and $V(\tau_d)$
have bounded intersection $d_X(\tau_c, \tau_d)$ is also bounded and
the claim is proved. 
\end{proof}

Now fix $i \in I_X$. 

\begin{claim*}
If $X$ is an annulus:
\begin{itemize}
\item
The core curve $\alpha$ is carried by and is wide in $\tau_i$.
\item
Both sides of $\alpha$ are combed in the induced track $\tau_i|X$.
\item
If $i+1 \in I_X$ then $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is obtained by taking subtracks,
slides, or at most a pair of splittings of $\tau_i|X$.
\end{itemize}
\end{claim*}

\begin{proof}
Since $i \in I_X$, both $\mathcal{A}(\tau_i|X)$ and $\mathcal{A}^*(\tau_i|X)$ have
diameter at least nine.  From Lemma~\ref{Lem:AnnulusBound} deduce that the
inclusions $V \subset \mathcal{A}$ and $V^* \subset \mathcal{A}^*$ are strict.
Thus by Lemma~\ref{Lem:AnnulusEquality} the core curve $\alpha$ is both
carried by and dual to $\tau_i|X$.  The second statement now follows
from Lemma~\ref{Lem:Combed}.  Thus at least one side of $\alpha$ is combed in
$\tau_i^X$.  Projecting from $S^X$ to $S$ we find that $\alpha \prec
\tau_i$.  If $\alpha$ is not wide in $\tau_i$ then we deduce that
neither side of $\alpha$ is combed in $\tau^X$, a contradiction.

Suppose that $\tau_i$ slides to $\tau_{i+1}$.  Then, up to isotopy,
$\tau_{i+1}$ slides to $\tau_i$.  Since slides do not kill essential
arcs it follows that $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is obtained from $\tau_i|X$ by an
at most countable collection of slides. 

Now suppose that $\tau_{i+1}$ is obtained by splitting $\tau_i$ along
a large branch $b$.  Thus $\tau_{i+1}^X$ is obtained from $\tau_i^X$
by splitting all of the countably many lifts of $b$.  Every essential
arc carried by $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is also carried by $\tau_i^X$.  Let
$\tau' \subset \tau_i^X$ be the union of these essential routes.  It
follows that $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is obtained from $\tau'$ by splitting
along lifts of $b$ that are also large branches of $\tau'$.  Since
both sides of $\alpha$ are combed in $\tau_i|X$ the same is true in
$\tau'$ and so any component of $\tau' {\smallsetminus} \alpha$ is a tree
without large branches.  The track $\tau'$ therefore has only finitely
many large branches, all contained in $\alpha$.  Since $\alpha$ is
wide in $\tau_i$ there are at most two preimages of the large branch
$b$ contained in $\alpha \subset S^X$.  Thus $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is
obtained from $\tau'$ by at most two splittings.  This proves the
claim.  (See Figure~\ref{Fig:Meet} for pictures of how $\alpha$ may be carried
by $\tau_i$ and how splitting $b$ effects $\tau_i|X$.)
\end{proof}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
$$\begin{array}{cc}
\includegraphics[height=3cm]{widelarge00} &
\includegraphics[height=3cm]{widelarge01} \\
\\
\includegraphics[height=3cm]{widelarge10} &
\includegraphics[height=3cm]{widelarge11} 
\end{array}$$
\caption{Four of the possible ways for an oriented, carried, wide
  curve $\alpha$ to meet a large rectangle $R_b$ of $N(\tau)$.  Note
  that when $X$ is an annulus and $\alpha$ is the core curve the upper
  left picture implies that neither side of $\alpha$ is combed in
  $\tau|X$.  Splitting the upper right deletes zero or two components
  of $\tau_i|X {\smallsetminus} \alpha$.  In the bottom row, only the left
  splitting is possible when $i, i+1 \in I_X$.  On the bottom left one
  component of $\tau_i|X {\smallsetminus} \alpha$ is deleted and $\tau_i|X$
  is split once.  On the bottom right $\tau_i|X$ is split twice.}
\label{Fig:Meet}
\end{figure}

\begin{claim*}
Suppose $X$ is not an annulus. 
\begin{itemize}
\item
When in efficient position
                                       
$\partial X$ is wide with respect to $\tau_i$.
\item
The track $\tau_i|X$ is birecurrent and fills $X$.
\item
If $i+1 \in I_X$ then $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is either a subtrack, a slide, or
a split of $\tau_i|X$.
\end{itemize}
\end{claim*}

\begin{proof}
Since $i \in I_X$ the second conclusion of Lemma~\ref{Lem:GeneralBound}
implies that $\partial X$ is wide.  The induced track $\tau_i|X$ carries a
pair of curves at distance at least three, so fills $X$.  Also,
$\tau_i|X$ is recurrent by definition.  For any branch $b' \in
\tau_i|X \subset S^X$, let $b \subset \tau$ be the image in $S$.
Since $\tau$ is transversely recurrent there is a dual curve $\beta$
meeting $b$.  Lifting $\beta$ to a curve or arc $\beta' \subset S^X$
gives a dual to $\tau|X$ meeting $b'$.  Thus $\tau|X$ is transversely
recurrent with respect to arcs and curves, as defined in
Section~\ref{Sec:InducedForNonAnnuli}

Now, if $\tau_i$ slides to $\tau_{i+1}$ then, as in the annulus case,
$\tau_i|X$ slides to $\tau_{i+1}|X$.  Suppose instead that $\tau_i$
splits to $\tau_{i+1}$ along the branch $b \in \mathcal{B}(\tau_i)$.  Thus
$\tau_i|X$ splits (or isotopes) to a track $\tau'$ so that
$\tau_{i+1}|X$ is a subtrack.  Let $R_b \subset N(\tau_i)$ be the
rectangle corresponding to the branch $b$.  Isotope $\partial X$ into
efficient position with respect to $N(\tau_i)$ and recall that $X$ is
to the left of $\partial X$.  Note that, by an isotopy, we may arrange for
all curves in $\mathcal{C}(\tau_i|X)$ to be disjoint from $\partial X$.  Let
$\beta \subset R_b$ be a {\em central splitting arc}: a carried arc
completely contained in $R_b$.

If $\beta \cap X$ is empty then $\tau_i|X$ is identical to
$\tau_{i+1}|X$.  If $\beta \subset X$ then $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is either a
subtrack or a splitting of $\tau_i|X$, depending how the carried
curves of $\tau_i|X$ meet the lift of $R_b$.  In all other cases
$\tau_{i+1}|X$ is a subtrack of $\tau_i|X$.  See Figure~\ref{Fig:Meet} for
some of the ways carried subarcs of $\partial X$ may meet $R_b$.  If $\partial
X \cap R_b$ contains a tie then $\tau_i|X$ is identical to
$\tau_{i+1}|X$.  This completes the proof of the claim.
\end{proof}

\noindent
Thus Theorem~\ref{Thm:FellowTravel} is proved.

$\mathcal{AC}^*(\tau_b^X)$ but may not be wide there.  If $\alpha^*$ is an arc

$\gamma^*$ which is either a wide dual arc to $\tau_b^X$ or is an
essential non-peripheral dual curve to $\tau_b^X$.  (If $\alpha^*$ is
a curve then let $\gamma^* = \alpha^*$.)  So $i(\alpha^*, \gamma^*)
\leq 2$ and thus $d_X(\alpha^*, \gamma^*) \leq 4$.  If $\gamma^*$ is a
wide dual arc then Lemma~\ref{Lem:GeneralBound} implies that $d_X(\gamma^*,
\beta') \leq {\sf K_1}$ and so $d_X(\alpha, \beta) \leq 2{\sf K_1} + 4$.  If
$\gamma^*$ is a dual curve then, as $b \mathbin{\notin} I_X$, any dual wide curve
$\delta^* \in V^*(\tau_b|X)$ has $d_X(\gamma^*, \delta^*) \leq 2$.
Again, Lemma~\ref{Lem:GeneralBound} implies that $d_X(\delta^*, \beta') \leq
{\sf K_1}$ and so $d_X(\alpha, \beta) \leq 2{\sf K_1} + 6$.

\begin{case}
Suppose $a \leq n_X < c < m_X \leq b$.
\end{case}

The first two cases bound $d_X(\tau_c, \tau_b)$ and $d_X(\tau_a,
\tau_c)$; thus we are done by the triangle inequality.

\begin{case}
Suppose $a \leq n_X < m_X \leq b$ and $m_X = n_X + 1$.
\end{case}

Let $c = n_X$ and $d = m_X$.  The first two cases bound $d_X(\tau_d,
\tau_b)$ and $d_X(\tau_a, \tau_c)$.  Since $V(\tau_c)$ and $V(\tau_d)$
have bounded intersection $d_X(\tau_c, \tau_d)$ is also bounded and
the claim is proved.

title: Claim
body_md:
If $X$ is an annulus:
\begin{itemize}
\item
The core curve $\alpha$ is carried by and is wide in $\tau_i$.
\item
Both sides of $\alpha$ are combed in the induced track $\tau_i|X$.
\item
If $i+1 \in I_X$ then $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is obtained by taking subtracks,
slides, or at most a pair of splittings of $\tau_i|X$.
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $i \in I_X$, both $\mathcal{A}(\tau_i|X)$ and $\mathcal{A}^*(\tau_i|X)$ have
diameter at least nine.  From Lemma~\ref{Lem:AnnulusBound} deduce that the
inclusions $V \subset \mathcal{A}$ and $V^* \subset \mathcal{A}^*$ are strict.
Thus by Lemma~\ref{Lem:AnnulusEquality} the core curve $\alpha$ is both
carried by and dual to $\tau_i|X$.  The second statement now follows
from Lemma~\ref{Lem:Combed}.  Thus at least one side of $\alpha$ is combed in
$\tau_i^X$.  Projecting from $S^X$ to $S$ we find that $\alpha \prec
\tau_i$.  If $\alpha$ is not wide in $\tau_i$ then we deduce that
neither side of $\alpha$ is combed in $\tau^X$, a contradiction.

Suppose that $\tau_i$ slides to $\tau_{i+1}$.  Then, up to isotopy,
$\tau_{i+1}$ slides to $\tau_i$.  Since slides do not kill essential
arcs it follows that $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is obtained from $\tau_i|X$ by an
at most countable collection of slides. 

Now suppose that $\tau_{i+1}$ is obtained by splitting $\tau_i$ along
a large branch $b$.  Thus $\tau_{i+1}^X$ is obtained from $\tau_i^X$
by splitting all of the countably many lifts of $b$.  Every essential
arc carried by $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is also carried by $\tau_i^X$.  Let
$\tau' \subset \tau_i^X$ be the union of these essential routes.  It
follows that $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is obtained from $\tau'$ by splitting
along lifts of $b$ that are also large branches of $\tau'$.  Since
both sides of $\alpha$ are combed in $\tau_i|X$ the same is true in
$\tau'$ and so any component of $\tau' {\smallsetminus} \alpha$ is a tree
without large branches.  The track $\tau'$ therefore has only finitely
many large branches, all contained in $\alpha$.  Since $\alpha$ is
wide in $\tau_i$ there are at most two preimages of the large branch
$b$ contained in $\alpha \subset S^X$.  Thus $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is
obtained from $\tau'$ by at most two splittings.  This proves the
claim.  (See Figure~\ref{Fig:Meet} for pictures of how $\alpha$ may be carried
by $\tau_i$ and how splitting $b$ effects $\tau_i|X$.)

title: Claim
body_md:
Suppose $X$ is not an annulus. 
\begin{itemize}
\item
When in efficient position
                                       
$\partial X$ is wide with respect to $\tau_i$.
\item
The track $\tau_i|X$ is birecurrent and fills $X$.
\item
If $i+1 \in I_X$ then $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is either a subtrack, a slide, or
a split of $\tau_i|X$.
\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $i \in I_X$ the second conclusion of Lemma~\ref{Lem:GeneralBound}
implies that $\partial X$ is wide.  The induced track $\tau_i|X$ carries a
pair of curves at distance at least three, so fills $X$.  Also,
$\tau_i|X$ is recurrent by definition.  For any branch $b' \in
\tau_i|X \subset S^X$, let $b \subset \tau$ be the image in $S$.
Since $\tau$ is transversely recurrent there is a dual curve $\beta$
meeting $b$.  Lifting $\beta$ to a curve or arc $\beta' \subset S^X$
gives a dual to $\tau|X$ meeting $b'$.  Thus $\tau|X$ is transversely
recurrent with respect to arcs and curves, as defined in
Section~\ref{Sec:InducedForNonAnnuli}

Now, if $\tau_i$ slides to $\tau_{i+1}$ then, as in the annulus case,
$\tau_i|X$ slides to $\tau_{i+1}|X$.  Suppose instead that $\tau_i$
splits to $\tau_{i+1}$ along the branch $b \in \mathcal{B}(\tau_i)$.  Thus
$\tau_i|X$ splits (or isotopes) to a track $\tau'$ so that
$\tau_{i+1}|X$ is a subtrack.  Let $R_b \subset N(\tau_i)$ be the
rectangle corresponding to the branch $b$.  Isotope $\partial X$ into
efficient position with respect to $N(\tau_i)$ and recall that $X$ is
to the left of $\partial X$.  Note that, by an isotopy, we may arrange for
all curves in $\mathcal{C}(\tau_i|X)$ to be disjoint from $\partial X$.  Let
$\beta \subset R_b$ be a {\em central splitting arc}: a carried arc
completely contained in $R_b$.

If $\beta \cap X$ is empty then $\tau_i|X$ is identical to
$\tau_{i+1}|X$.  If $\beta \subset X$ then $\tau_{i+1}|X$ is either a
subtrack or a splitting of $\tau_i|X$, depending how the carried
curves of $\tau_i|X$ meet the lift of $R_b$.  In all other cases
$\tau_{i+1}|X$ is a subtrack of $\tau_i|X$.  See Figure~\ref{Fig:Meet} for
some of the ways carried subarcs of $\partial X$ may meet $R_b$.  If $\partial
X \cap R_b$ contains a tie then $\tau_i|X$ is identical to
$\tau_{i+1}|X$.  This completes the proof of the claim.

label: Thm:Unparam
title: Theorem
body_md:
\cite[Theorem~1.3]{MasurMinsky04}
\label{Thm:Unparam}
For any surface $S$ with $\xi(S) \geq 1$ there is a constant $Q =
Q(S)$ with the following property: For any sliding and splitting
sequence $\{ \tau_i \}_{i=0}^N$ of birecurrent train tracks in $S$ the
sequence $\{ V(\tau_i) \}_{i=0}^N$ forms a $Q$--unparameterized
quasi-geodesic in $\mathcal{C}(S)$.
head: environment

label: Thm:LocalUnparam
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Thm:LocalUnparam}
For any surface $S$ with $\xi(S) \geq 1$ there is a constant $Q =
Q(S)$ with the following property: For any sliding and splitting
sequence $\{ \tau_i \}_{i=0}^N$ of birecurrent train tracks in $S$ and
for any essential subsurface $X \subset S$ if $\pi_X(\tau_N) \neq
\emptyset$ then the sequence $\{ \pi_X(\tau_i) \}_{i=0}^N$ is a
$Q$--unparameterized quasi-geodesic in $\mathcal{C}(X)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the first conclusion of Theorem~\ref{Thm:FellowTravel} we may restrict
attention to the subinterval $[p,q] = I_X \subset [0,N]$.

Fix any vertex $\alpha \in V(\tau_q|X)$.  Note $\alpha$ is carried by
$\tau_i|X$ for all $i \leq q$.  So define $\sigma_i \subset \tau_i|X$
to be the minimal pretrack carrying $\alpha$.  Since $\sigma_i$ does
not carry any peripheral curves $\sigma_i$ is a train track.  Note
that $\sigma_i$ is recurrent by definition and transversely recurrent
by Lemma~\ref{Lem:TransverseRecurrenceAC}.  Applying Theorem~\ref{Thm:FellowTravel},
for all $i \in [p, q-1]$ the track $\sigma_{i+1}$ is a slide, a split,
or identical to the track $\sigma_i$.

Theorem~\ref{Thm:Unparam} implies the sequence $\{ V(\sigma_i) \}$ is a
$Q$--unparameterized quasi-geodesic in $\mathcal{C}(X)$.  Note that
$d_X(\sigma_i, \tau_i|X)$ is uniformly bounded because $\sigma_i$ is a
subtrack.

Since $\alpha \prec \tau_i|X$ the curve $\alpha$ is also carried by
$\tau_i$.  By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Decompose} there is a vertex cycle $\beta_i
\prec \tau_i$ that cuts $X$.  Since $\beta_i$ is wide
(Lemma~\ref{Lem:VerticesWide}) any element $\beta_i' \in \pi_X(\beta)$ is
carried by and wide in $\tau_i^X$.  It follows that $\beta_i'$ and the
vertex cycles of $\tau_i|X$ have bounded intersection.  Thus
$d_X(\tau_i, \tau_i|X)$ is uniformly bounded and we are done.

label: Lem:Slide
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\{ \tau_i \}$ be the given sliding and splitting sequence in
$\mathcal{T}(S)$.  Let $I = [p,q] \subset [0,N]$ be a subinterval.  Note
that $d_{\mathcal{T}(S)}(I) \leq |I|$ because $\{ \tau_i \}$ is an edge-path
in $\mathcal{T}(S)$.

Define $\mathcal{S}(I)$ to be the set of indices $r \in I$ where $r + 1 \in
I$ and $\tau_{r+1}$ is a splitting of $\tau_r$.  Thus $|I| \leq_A
|\mathcal{S}(I)|$, where $A$ is the constant of Lemma~\ref{Lem:Slide}.  Now,
Theorem~\ref{Thm:Quasi} implies $|\mathcal{S}(I)| \leq_Q d_{\mathcal{M}(S)}(I)$.  Finally,
since $\tau \mapsto V(\tau)$ is distance non-increasing we have
$d_{\mathcal{M}(S)}(I) \leq d_{\mathcal{T}(S)}(I)$.  Deduce that $|I| \leq_Q
d_{\mathcal{M}(S)}(I)$, for a somewhat larger value of $Q$.

title: Theorem

label: Lem:Reverse
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:Reverse}
For every $\delta$ and $Q$, there is a constant ${\sf R_0} =
{\sf R_0}(\delta, Q)$ with the following property: For any
$\delta$--hyperbolic space $\mathcal{X}$, for any $Q$--unparameterized
quasi-geodesic $f \colon [m,n] \to \mathcal{X}$, and for any $a, b, c \in
[m,n]$, if $a \leq b \leq c$ then
\[
d_\mathcal{X}(\alpha, \beta) + d_\mathcal{X}(\beta, \gamma) 
    \leq d_\mathcal{X}(\alpha, \gamma) + {\sf R_0}
\]
where $\alpha, \beta, \gamma = f(a), f(b), f(c)$. \qed

title: Theorem

\[

label: Def:Induct
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Def:Induct}
Suppose that $Y \subset X$ is an essential subsurface with $\xi(Y) <
\xi(X)$.  If $d_Y(J_X) \geq {\sf T_0}(X)$ then we call $Y$ an {\em
inductive} subsurface of $X$ and take $J_Y = I_Y \cap J_X$ as the
associated {\em inductive subinterval} of $J_X$.  If $d_Y(J_X) <
{\sf T_0}(X)$ then we set $J_Y = \emptyset$.
head: environment

label: Def:Straight
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{Def:Straight}
A subinterval $I \subset J_X$ is a {\em straight subinterval} for
$X$ if for all essential subsurfaces $Y \subset X$, with $\xi(Y) <
\xi(X)$, we have $\operatorname{diam}_Y(I) \leq {\sf T_1}(X)$.
head: environment

label: Lem:Disjoint
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix an essential $Y \subset X$ with $\xi(Y) < \xi(X)$.  It suffices to
show, for every subinterval $J \subset I$, that $d_Y(J) \leq
{\sf T_1}(X)$.

If $J \cap I_Y = \emptyset$ then Theorem~\ref{Thm:FellowTravel} implies $d_Y(J)
\leq {\sf K_0}$.
                            
Suppose that $J$ meets $I_Y$; thus $J_Y = \emptyset$ by hypothesis and
so $Y$ is not inductive.  It follows that $d_Y(I) < {\sf T_0}(X)$.  By
Lemma~\ref{Lem:Reverse} we have $d_Y(J) < {\sf T_0}(X) + 2{\sf R_0}$.

label: Lem:Straight
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $X$ is an annulus then, by Theorem~\ref{Thm:FellowTravel}, for every $r \in
I$ the core curve $\alpha \subset X$ is carried by and wide in
$\tau_r$.  It follows that the number of switches in $\alpha \subset
\tau_r|X$ is bounded by some constant $K = K(S)$.  Let $q = \max I$
and pick any $\beta \in V(\tau_q|X)$.  As in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{Thm:LocalUnparam} let $\sigma_r \subset \tau_r|X$ be the minimal
subtrack carrying $\beta$.  Thus $\sigma_r$ has either exactly four
branches and two switches, or is an embedded arc.  It follows that
every $K^2/4$ consecutive splittings in $S_X(I)$ induces at least one
splitting in the sequence of tracks $\{ \sigma_r \}$.  Therefore the
singleton sets $V(\sigma_r)$ form a quasi-geodesic in $\mathcal{A}(X)$.
Since $V(\sigma_r) \subset V(\tau_r|X)$ the proof is complete when $X$
is an annulus.

We assume for the rest of the proof that $X$ is not an annulus.  The
map $i \mapsto V(\tau_i|X)$, taking tracks to their vertex cycles, is
generally not injective.  (For example, see~\cite[Proposition
2.2.2]{PennerHarer92}.)  However:

\begin{claim}
\label{Clm:NoMotion}
There is a constant ${\sf N_0} = {\sf N_0}(X)$, independent of $\{ \tau_i \}$,
so that if $V(\tau_r|X) = V(\tau_s|X)$ then $|\mathcal{S}_X(r,s)| \leq
{\sf N_0}$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
Let $\mu = V(\tau_r|X)$.  Our hypothesis on $\tau_s|X$ and induction
proves that $V(\tau_t|X) = \mu$ for all $t \in [r,s]$.  Recurrence and
uniqueness of carrying \cite[Proposition 3.7.3]{Mosher03} implies that
$\tau_{t+1}|X$ is a split or a slide of $\tau_t|X$, and not a
subtrack, for all $t \in [r,s-1]$.

If $t \in [r,s]$ and $b \in \mathcal{B}(\tau_t|X)$ then define $w_\mu(b) =
\sum_{\alpha \in \mu} w_\alpha(b)$.  Let
\[
M(t) = 
   \big( w_\mu(b) :
         \mbox{$b$ is a large branch of $\tau_t|X$} \big) 
\]
be the sequence of given numbers, arranged in non-increasing order.
Note that if $\tau_{t+1}|X$ is a slide of $\tau_t|X$ then $M(t+1) =
M(t)$.  However, if $t \in \mathcal{S}_X(r, s)$ then the recurrence of
$\tau_t|X$ implies that $M(t+1) < M(t)$, in lexicographic order.
Since there are only finitely many possibilities for an induced track
$\tau|X$, up to the action of $\mathcal{MCG}(X)$, the claim follows.
                                                                     
\end{proof}

                   
                                                                     
                                                           
                                                                

                                                                 
                                                                      
                                                                        

                                                                      
                                                                 
                      

Notice that if $V(\tau_{i+1}|X) \neq V(\tau_i|X)$ then
$V(\tau_{i+1}|X) \neq V(\tau_j|X)$ for $j \leq i$.  This is because
$P(\tau_{k+1}|X) \subset P(\tau_k|X)$ for all $k$.  Using $C = 1 +
\max \{ {\sf C}(X), {\sf T_1}(X) \}$ as the cut-off in
Theorem~\ref{Thm:DistEst} gives some constant of quasi-equality, say
${\sf E}$. Define ${\sf R_1} = {\sf E} + 1$.

Suppose that $[p,q] = I$, the straight subinterval of $J_X$ given by
Lemma~\ref{Lem:Straight}.  We define a function $\rho \colon [0,M] \to I$ as
follows: let $\rho(0) = p$ and let $\rho(n+1)$ be the smallest element
in $[\rho(n), q]$ with $d_{\mathcal{M}(X)}(\tau_{\rho(n)}, \tau_{\rho(n+1)})
= {\sf R_1}$.  (If $\rho(n+1)$ is undefined then take $M = n+1$ and
$\rho(M) = q$.)  Let $B(\mu)$ be the ball of radius ${\sf R_1}$ about
the marking $\mu \in \mathcal{M}(X)$.  Define
\[
{\sf V} = \max \big\{ |B(\mu)| : \mu \in \mathcal{M}(X) \big\}.
\]
Deduce from Claim~\ref{Clm:NoMotion} and the remark immediately following
that, for all $n \in [0, M - 1]$,
\begin{gather*}
|\mathcal{S}_X(\rho(n), \rho(n+1))| \leq {\sf N_0} {\sf V}. \\
\tag*{\text{Thus}}
|\mathcal{S}_X(I)| \leq {\sf N_0} {\sf V} \cdot M.
\end{gather*}
So to prove Lemma~\ref{Lem:Straight} it suffices to bound $M$ from above in
terms of $d_X(I)$.

\begin{claim}
\label{Clm:Jump}
Fix $n \in [0,M-2]$.  Let $\tau, \sigma = \tau_{\rho(n)},
\tau_{\rho(n+1)}$.  Then $d_X(\tau, \sigma) \geq {\sf R_0} + 1$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
We use Theorem~\ref{Thm:DistEst}.  Note that $d_{\mathcal{M}(X)}(\tau, \sigma) =
{\sf R_1}$.  Since ${\sf R_1}$ is greater than the additive error there is
at least one non-vanishing term in the sum $\sum_{Y \subset X}
[d_Y(\tau, \sigma)]_C$.  

However, since $[\rho(n), \rho(n+1)] \subset [p,q]$ and $[p,q] = I$ is
straight we have $d_Y(\tau, \sigma) \leq {\sf T_1}(X)$ for all $Y
\subset X$ with $\xi(Y) < \xi(X)$.  Thus $d_X(\tau, \sigma)$ is the
only term of the sum greater than the cut-off $C$.  Since $C >
{\sf T_1}(X) \geq {\sf R_0}$, we have $d_X(\tau, \sigma) \geq {\sf R_0}
+ 1$ and the claim is proved.
                              
\end{proof}

Thus we have
\begin{align*}
d_X(I)    &\geq -(M - 1) \cdot {\sf R_0} + 
             \sum_{n = 0}^{M - 1} d_X(\tau_{\rho(n)}, \tau_{\rho(n+1)}) \\
          &\geq M - 1 + d_X(\tau_{\rho(M-1)}, \tau_{\rho(M)}) \\
          &\geq M - 1 
\end{align*}
where the first and second lines follow from Lemma~\ref{Lem:Reverse} and
Claim~\ref{Clm:Jump} respectively.  This completes the proof of
Lemma~\ref{Lem:Straight}.

label: Lem:StraightInInduct
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:StraightInInduct}
There is a constant $A = A(X)$ with the following property: Suppose
that $J_Y \subset J_X$ is an inductive interval.  Suppose that $I
\subset J_Y$ is a straight subinterval for $X$.  Then $|\mathcal{S}_X(I)|
\leq A$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $[p,q] = I$.  Applying Theorem~\ref{Thm:FellowTravel}, as $p \in J_Y
\subset I_Y$, the multicurve $\partial Y$ is wide with respect to
$\tau_p$.  It follows that $\partial Y$ is also wide with respect to
$\tau_p^X$.  Note that the curves of $V(\tau_p|X)$ are also wide with
respect to $\tau_p^X$.  Repeating this discussion for $q$, and then
applying Lemma~\ref{Lem:GeneralBound} and the triangle inequality gives a
uniform bound for $d_X(\tau_p, \tau_q)$.  The lemma now follows from
Lemma~\ref{Lem:Straight}.

label: Lem:LongBound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:LongBound}
There is a constant $A = A(X)$, independent of $\{ \tau_i \}$, so that
\[
\sum_{I \in {\sf Long}} |\mathcal{S}_X(I)| \leq_A d_X(J_X).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
From Lemma~\ref{Lem:Straight} we deduce
\[
\sum_{I \in {\sf Long}} |\mathcal{S}_X(I)| 
   \leq_A |{\sf Long}| + \sum_{I \in {\sf Long}} d_X(I) 
\]
where the first term on the right arises from addition of additive
errors.  
                                                                    
            
By the definition of a long straight interval and from
Lemma~\ref{Lem:Reverse} deduce
\[
4{\sf R_0}|{\sf Long}| \leq \sum_{I \in {\sf Long}} d_X(I) 
     \leq d_X(J_X) + 2{\sf R_0}|{\sf Long}|.
\]
Thus $2{\sf R_0}|{\sf Long}| \leq d_X(J_X)$.  These inequalities combine to
prove the lemma, for a somewhat larger value of $A = A(X)$.

There is a constant $A = A(X)$, independent of $\{ \tau_i \}$, so that

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{Lem:Straight} the number of splittings in any short straight
interval is a priori bounded (depending only on $X$).  Since $|{\sf Short}|
\leq |{\sf Ind}'|$ the lemma follows.

label: Lem:Nested
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $U \in {\sf Ind}$ contains $Z$.  Suppose $J_Z = [p,q]$ and
$J_X = [m,n]$.  Thus $\partial Z$ is wide with respect to $\tau_p$.  So
$d_U(\tau_p, \partial Z) \leq {\sf N_1}$, by the definition of
${\sf N_1}$, and the same holds at the index $q$.  Thus $d_U(\tau_p,
\tau_q) \leq 2{\sf N_1}$.  The subsurface $U$ {\em precedes} or {\em
succeeds} $Z$ if $d_U(\tau_m, \tau_p)$ or $d_U(\tau_q, \tau_n)$,
respectively, is greater than or equal to $2{\sf N_1} + {\sf N_2} +
{\sf K_0}(X) + 1$.  Note that $U$ must precede or succeed $Z$ (or both)
as otherwise $d_U(\tau_m, \tau_n) < 6{\sf N_1} + 2{\sf N_2} +
2{\sf K_0}(X) + 2 \leq {\sf T_0}(X)$, a contradiction.
                                                            

It now suffices to consider subsurfaces $U$ and $V$ that both succeed
and both contain $Z$.  If $\max J_U \leq \max J_V$ then $U \subset V$.
For, if not, $\partial V$ cuts $U$ while missing $Z$.  Since $\partial V$ is
wide at the index $r = \max J_V$ we deduce that
\begin{align*}
d_U(\tau_q, \tau_n) 
  \leq {} & d_U(\tau_q, \partial Z) + d_U(\partial Z, \partial V) 
            + d_U(\partial V, \tau_r) + \\
          & + d_U(\tau_r, \tau_{r+1}) + d_U(\tau_{r+1}, \tau_n) \\
  \leq {} & 2{\sf N_1} + {\sf N_2} + {\sf K_0}(X) + 1
\end{align*}
and this is a contradiction.  Thus the surfaces in ${\sf Ind}$ that
strictly contain $Z$, and succeed $Z$, are nested.

label: Lem:InductiveBound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Lem:InductiveBound}
There is a constant $A = A(X)$, independent of $\{ \tau_i \}$, so that
the number of splittings contained in inductive intervals is
quasi-bounded by $|{\sf Ind}| + \sum_{Y \in {\sf Ind}} d_Y(J_X)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $Y \in {\sf Ind}$.  Consider an index $r \in J_Y$ that is assigned to
$X$.  Let $I \subset J_Y$ be the maximal interval containing $r$ so
that all indices in $\mathcal{S}_X(I)$ are assigned to $X$.  We now show
that $I$ is straight.  Let $Z$ be any essential subsurface of $X$ with
$\xi(Z) < \xi(X)$ and let $[r,s] = J \subset I$ be any subinterval.
If $J \cap I_Z = \emptyset$ then Theorem~\ref{Thm:FellowTravel} implies that
$d_Z(J) \leq {\sf K_0}$.  If $J$ meets $I_Z$ then, as no splittings of
$J$ are assigned to $Z$ we deduce that $\tau_s|Z$ is obtained from
$\tau_r|Z$ by sliding and taking subtracks only.  Thus $d_Z(J) \leq
{\sf B_0} {\sf N_2} \leq {\sf T_1}(X)$, as desired.
                                       

By Lemma~\ref{Lem:StraightInInduct} we find that $|\mathcal{S}_X(I)|$ is
bounded.  It follows that the number of splittings in the inductive
intervals is quasi-bounded by $\sum_{Y \in {\sf Ind}} |\mathcal{S}_Y(J_Y)|$.

By induction, Proposition~\ref{Prop:Induct} gives 
\[
|\mathcal{S}_Y(J_Y)| \leq_A d_{\mathcal{M}(Y)}(J_Y).  
\]
Taking a cutoff of $C = 1 + \max \{ {\sf C}(Y), {\sf T_0}(X) + 2{\sf R_0}
\}$ and applying the distance estimate Theorem~\ref{Thm:DistEst} we have a
quasi-inequality
\[
d_{\mathcal{M}(Y)}(J_Y) \, \leq_{\sf E} \sum_{Z \subset Y} [d_Z(J_Y)]_C.
\]
Since $d_Z(J_Y) \leq d_Z(J_X) + 2{\sf R_0}$ for all $Z \subset Y$, it
follows that non-zero terms in the sum only arise for subsurfaces in
${\sf Ind}'(Y) = \{ Z \in {\sf Ind}' \mathbin{\mid} Z \subset Y \}$.  Since $2{\sf R_0} \leq
{\sf T_0}(X)$
                             
we have $[d_Z(J_Y)]_C \leq 2\cdot d_Z(J_X)$.  Making $A = A(X)$ larger
if necessary we have
\begin{align*}
|\mathcal{S}_Y(J_Y)| 
  &\leq_A \sum_{Z \in {\sf Ind}'(Y)} d_Z(J_X). \\
\tag*{\text{Thus}}
\sum_{Y \in {\sf Ind}} |\mathcal{S}_Y(J_Y)| 
  &\leq_A |{\sf Ind}| + \sum_{Y \in {\sf Ind}} 
                       \sum_{Z \in {\sf Ind}'(Y)} d_Z(J_X) \\
  &\leq_{A} |{\sf Ind}| + \sum_{Y \in {\sf Ind}} d_Y(J_X) 
\end{align*}
where the final quasi-inequality follows from Lemma~\ref{Lem:Nested}, taking
$A$ larger as necessary.  Note that the term $|{\sf Ind}|$ on the middle
line arises by adding additive errors.  This proves
Lemma~\ref{Lem:InductiveBound}.
